hook.support: Something goes wrong at work. Someone slips. A machine sparks. What do you write down? A good report says what happened. Then it can be fixed.
hook.core: Someone slips on a wet floor at work. Nobody is badly hurt, so nobody writes it down. Next week, someone else slips, and this time they break a wrist. An incident report is how a workplace learns from what goes wrong, before it goes wrong again.
hook.extend: An incident report is a record that a workplace can act on. If it’s vague, full of blame or never written, the same hazard waits for the next person. Learn to write one that is clear, factual and useful.

why.support: Reports help stop the same thing happening again.
why.core: Most workplaces have to record incidents. A clear report protects you, your workmates and the business.
why.extend: Reports feed safety decisions, insurance claims and legal records. The quality of the writing decides whether anyone can act on it.

articles.title: Write it down, get it fixed

body.support:
An **incident** is when someone gets hurt, or could have. A **near miss** is when nobody was hurt, but they could have been.

**First, be safe.**
- Make the area safe.
- Get first aid if someone is hurt.
- Tell your supervisor.
.
**Then write a report.** Most workplaces have a form. It asks:
- What happened?
- When and where?
- Who was hurt? Who saw it?
- Was anything damaged?
- What did you do?
.
**Write facts, not opinions.** A **fact** can be checked. An **opinion** is what someone thinks.

- Fact: The floor near the sink was wet.
- Opinion: Sam is careless.
.
Use full sentences. Write in the order things happened. Check your spelling. Sign and date it.
body.core:
An **incident** is any event at work that hurts someone, or could have. A **near miss** is an incident where nobody was hurt, but they could have been. Both should be reported.

**First, make it safe.** Remove the **hazard** if you can, get first aid, and tell your supervisor.

**Then report it.** Most workplaces use a set form, so every report has the same parts:
- **Details:** date, time and exact place.
- **People:** who was involved, and any **witnesses**.
- **What happened:** the events, in order.
- **Injury or damage:** what and how bad.
- **Action taken:** what was done straight away, and what should change.
- **Sign-off:** your name, signature and the date.

**Who reads it?** Your supervisor, a safety officer, maybe an insurer or WorkSafe. They weren’t there. The report has to tell them exactly what happened.

**How to write it:**
- Stick to **facts**: things that can be checked. Leave out **opinions** and blame.
- Use full sentences, in time order.
- Be exact. “At 2:15 pm” is better than “in the afternoon”.
- Check spelling and punctuation. A report may be read in court.
body.extend:
An **incident** is any work event that causes harm, or could have. A **near miss** is one where harm was avoided, often by luck. Safety experts treat near misses as warnings, so most workplaces require them to be reported.

**First, make it safe:** control the **hazard**, give first aid and notify a supervisor. Serious incidents must also be reported to WorkSafe Victoria.

**Structure.** Report forms follow a set structure, so readers can find information fast and compare reports:
- **details:** date, time and exact location.
- **people:** those involved, and **witnesses**.
- **description:** what happened, in time order.
- **injury or damage**.
- **action taken:** immediate response and suggested changes.
- **sign-off:** name, signature, date.

**Audience and purpose.** Readers include supervisors, safety staff, insurers, regulators and sometimes courts. None of them were there. The purpose is to record what happened, so the cause can be fixed.

**Language.** Keep the report **objective**:
- facts that can be checked, not opinions or blame.
- past tense, in time order.
- precise times, places and measures.
- correct sentences, punctuation and spelling.

A report that blames a person often hides the real cause. That might be a missing sign, poor training or a broken process.

caseStudies.title: The warnings nobody passed on

body.support:
In **September 1998**, there was an explosion at a gas plant at **Longford**, in Gippsland, Victoria.

**Two workers died.** Eight more were hurt. Much of Victoria had no gas for about **two weeks**.

A **Royal Commission** looked into what went wrong. It found the company, **Esso**, was at fault. The workers were not to blame.

The Commission found there had been **warning signs**. A similar problem happened a few weeks before. But it was not reported to the right people. So nothing was fixed.

The lesson: report problems, even small ones. Someone needs to know.
body.core:
On **25 September 1998**, an explosion and fire tore through the Esso gas plant at **Longford**, in Gippsland, Victoria.

**Two workers were killed** and eight were injured. Gas to most of Victoria was cut off for about **two weeks**. Homes had no hot water. Many businesses had to close.

The Victorian Government set up a **Royal Commission**. It found that **Esso**, the company, was responsible, not the workers at the plant. Workers had not been trained for what happened.

The Commission also found **warning signs**. A similar problem had happened on **28 August**, less than a month before. It was not reported to the people who could have acted on it.

If warnings aren’t written down and passed on, a workplace can’t learn from them.
body.extend:
On **25 September 1998**, an explosion and fire destroyed part of the Esso gas plant at **Longford**, in Gippsland. **Two workers were killed** and eight injured. Victoria’s gas supply was cut for about **two weeks**, shutting down homes and industry.

A **Royal Commission** found that **Esso**, the company, was responsible, rather than the operators on shift. Workers had not been trained to deal with the conditions that led to the blast.

The Commission also found **warning signs** that went nowhere. A similar incident on **28 August**, less than a month earlier, was not reported to the people who could have acted on it.

Safety researcher Andrew Hopkins studied the disaster in his book *Lessons from Longford*. A key lesson is that a reporting system is only useful if people use it, and if reports reach someone who acts.

Incident reports are how a workplace remembers. Without them, the same hazard can strike twice.

source.name: Australian Institute for Disaster Resilience — Longford gas explosion, September 1998

teacher.overview: Students learn what incidents and near misses are, what to do first, the six-part structure of an incident report, who reads reports, and how to write objectively (facts, not opinions or blame; time order; precise details; correct conventions). The case study is the 1998 Esso Longford gas explosion, where a Royal Commission found the company responsible and that an earlier warning sign wasn’t reported to people who could act. The final mission is a written incident report.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 exact date, time and place; 2 people by role, plus a witness; 3 objective description in past tense, no blame; 4 injury or damage; 5 immediate action and fixing the cause; 6 sign-off (who and when).

**Sort:** facts — box fell at 3:05 pm; nobody hurt; shelf had no lip. Opinions — “stacks like an idiot”; “disaster waiting to happen”; “management never listens” (a real concern, but for a different channel).

**Case study:** an explosion and fire at the Esso gas plant at Longford on 25 September 1998 killed two workers and injured eight, and cut Victoria’s gas for about two weeks; the Royal Commission found Esso responsible, not the operators; a similar incident on 28 August wasn’t reported to people who could act.
realityCheck: **Longford is close to home in Gippsland.** Some families lost people or jobs. Don’t name the workers who died, and handle questions gently.
**Students will want to write “it was his fault”.** The sort is where that habit gets broken. Ask “could a camera check that?”
**Some sources give the gas outage as 10 to 19 days.** The course says “about two weeks”.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students with jobs often recognise their own workplace’s form.
